title: The Dragon structure: pawn skeleton, half-open files and the breaks each side wants
outcomes: Names the half-open files of the Dragon (c for Black, d for White) and says which pawn trade created each
Finds each side's pawn lever (d, b and a for Black; g and h for White) and says which file it opens
Says what each lever needs to be true (rook behind the b-pawn, bishop on c8 for d5, king safe before the h-file opens)
Recognises a position where no lever is ready and chooses a quiet move, and a position where a quiet move is a mistake

steps.prompt: Whose attack do you think arrives first, and why? Write the reason, not just the name of the side. You will come back to this at the end.

steps.text: **Today's question.** Both kings are castled, but on opposite wings. A rule of thumb from Edward Lasker: with kings on opposite wings, speed counts more than material, because pawns stop being a shield and become a battering ram. We will test it. By the end you will say, for each side, which pawn lever it wants, which file it opens, and what to do when it is blocked or early. First, three small positions.

steps.text: **The skeleton.** Pieces can leave a square; pawns cannot go back, so the pawns fix the rest of the game (Edward Lasker, *Chess Strategy*). Black's c-pawn is gone, and no black pawn can ever guard h6. White's d-pawn is gone, and no white pawn can ever guard e3. [I] In the main line Black pushes the h-pawn to h5, which blocks White's h-pawn on h4 until the g-pawn offers a trade.

steps.caption: Only the pawns and kings, taken from the Dragon position. Each side has one hole on a dark square: h6 for Black, e3 for White.

steps.text: **The levers.** A lever is a pawn push that challenges an enemy pawn or piece, to change the pawn structure or open a line. Black has three: the d-pawn hits e4; the b-pawn and the a-pawn need two moves each, to reach b4 and a4 and hit c3 and b3. White has two: the h-pawn (aimed at g6) and the g-pawn (kicks the knight on f6). A queen move or a rook given up on c3 are non-pawn ideas, not levers.

steps.caption: Black's three pawn levers on the skeleton. Each arrow is a legal pawn move. The d-pawn hits the e4 pawn at once; the b-pawn and a-pawn head for b4 and a4, from where they would hit c3 and b3.

steps.text: **When ...d5 works.** In this position it needs d5 defended twice. [I] With the bishop on c8, the knight on f6 and the queen (through d7) defend d5; with the bishop on d7 only the knight does, so Nxd5 wins a pawn. We did not test the knight on c6. [H] ...d5 is a freeing move more than a plan. Weak evidence: of 199 master games with it, 97 were drawn (61 White wins, 41 Black wins).

steps.text: **The break that comes too early.** The h-pawn lever is not a command. Here the capture on g6 opens the file but leaves the white king on c1 with a2 as a target, and the engine prefers a quiet king move first. [I] A rule of thumb: before you open a file, make sure the king can stand the counter-blow.

steps.text: **Why the h-pawn lever works.** [H] I think it works less because the black king is weak than because h6 is a hole: no black pawn can ever guard it, so a white bishop can land there and a rook can follow down the opened file. Test it before you push: does the hole exist, and does a black piece or pawn block the file?

steps.text: **Black's plans, and what must be true.** Put a rook on the half-open c-file, then pick a lever. The boards showed: the d-pawn lever needs d5 defended enough, and the b-pawn lever needs its pawn defended after the push (here by the bishop on d7). [I] A rook behind the lever probably helps; not tested. [H] The a-pawn lever wants a piece to hit; not tested. A quiet move at the wrong moment can lose the race.

steps.caption: White's chain runs e4, f3, g2: the head is e4 and the base is g2. Nimzowitsch advised attacking the base of a chain, not its head (My System), a long-term siege that matters most in endgames. [I] In the Dragon the ...d5 lever hits the head, and that attack is the faster one. White's pawn on h4 starts the lever and keeps the black h-pawn from marching down to the base.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. Write four sentences for a beginner who knows how the pieces move: (1) what a pawn lever is, (2) when it works, (3) one example they could set up on a board, (4) one warning. Then go back to your first guess and ask it again: whose attack is faster, and by how many moves?

steps.text: **Self-check.** Did you say when the lever works? When it fails? Did you give an example a beginner could set up on a board? Did you name one mistake? Nothing here is graded by the app. If you can answer all four, you can teach this part of the Dragon.

**What to remember.**
The pawns last; the pieces move around them.
Black's c-file and White's d-file are half-open because a pawn was traded.
Black's levers: d, b, a. White's levers: h, g.
A lever needs support: the pushed pawn defended, the king safe.
With opposite kings pawns are cheap, but a quiet move can cost a pawn.
[I] With both kings on one wing the plans change.
